messages.content: Write a Python worker that pulls items off a queue.Queue in a thread and processes each with a callback. Around 50 lines.

`worker.py` (61 lines, smoke-tested above):

- `Worker(callback, q=None)` — owns a `queue.Queue` unless you pass one in.
- The thread is a daemon, so a stuck worker never blocks interpreter shutdown.
- Callback exceptions are logged and swallowed; `task_done()` fires in a `finally` so a raising callback cannot deadlock `join()`.
- `stop()` pushes a private sentinel rather than flipping a flag, so it never has to poll with a `get(timeout=...)` and wakes immediately.
- Usable as a context manager: `with Worker(fn) as w: ...` starts on entry and drains-then-stops on exit.

One thing to know: `stop()` only drains items queued *before* it — anything `put()` after the sentinel is discarded with the queue. If you want a hard cancel that drops the backlog, that needs a separate flag checked in the loop; say the word and I'll add it.

The repo already has `queue_worker.py` and `simple_queue_worker.py` covering the same ground at ~165 lines each, so I wrote to a new file instead of overwriting either.
Add a clean shutdown on a sentinel value.

`worker.py`, 93 lines. Smoke test above covers three cases; the traceback in the output is the expected logged exception from the raising-callback case.

What changed:

- `STOP` is now a module-level singleton (`_Stop` instance with a `repr` of `STOP`), so anyone holding the queue can signal shutdown: `q.put(STOP)`. That matters mainly when you pass your own queue in — the producer can close the stream without a reference to the `Worker`.
- The loop exits on `STOP` before calling the callback, so items queued ahead of it all run first. Shutdown drains, it does not cancel.
- `stop()` is idempotent and won't double-enqueue. It takes a lock, sets `_stopping`, and only sends the sentinel if the thread is still alive. Without that, a `stop()` after a producer-sent `STOP` would leave an unconsumed sentinel sitting in the queue and a later `join()` would block forever.
- Added a `running` property, since with sentinel shutdown the worker can now exit without you calling `stop()`.

Two caveats worth having in mind:

Anything `put()` after the sentinel is never processed. In the smoke test, `"never"` stays in the queue and `queue.join()` on that queue would block on it. If producers send `STOP` themselves, they own the ordering.

The `send = self._thread.is_alive()` check is a race in the narrow window where the thread is exiting: `is_alive()` can read true just as the loop returns, and the sentinel is then left in the queue. Closing it properly needs the thread to record its own exit under the same lock. Tell me if you want that tightened, or the hard-cancel flag I mentioned earlier.
An exception in the callback currently kills the thread silently. Handle it.

It's already handled, and the exception is not silent. `worker.py:62-63` wraps the callback in `except Exception` and logs with `logger.exception`; `task_done()` is in the `finally`, so the loop survives and `join()` doesn't hang. The run above raises on item 2 and the worker still processes 1 and 3 and stays alive — the traceback in that output is the log record, printed by logging's last-resort handler because the test configures no handlers.

I described this in both earlier passes, so I've left the file alone rather than re-adding what's there.

Two gaps that are real, if either is what you're after:

- A `BaseException` from the callback (not `Exception`) still kills the thread — `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit`, or a stray `GeneratorExit`. And when the thread dies, `queue.join()` on any later item blocks forever, with nothing recording why. A `try/finally` around the whole loop that stores the exit reason and marks the worker dead would turn that into a visible failure.
- Errors only go to `logger`. If you want per-item handling — a dead-letter queue, a retry, a metric — that needs an `on_error(item, exc)` hook instead of the bare log call.

Say which one and I'll add it.
Add a maximum in-flight count so a slow callback cannot back everything up.

output:
`worker.py`, 110 lines. All three cases above pass.

What changed:

- `Worker(callback, max_pending=N)` builds a bounded `queue.Queue(maxsize=N)`. `0` (the default) stays unbounded, matching `Queue`'s own convention. Passing both `q` and `max_pending` raises — the bound belongs to whichever queue object you own.
- `put(item, block=True, timeout=None)` now forwards those args, so a producer can block, time out, or fail fast. `try_put(item)` returns `False` instead of raising `queue.Full`.
- `pending` exposes `qsize()`.
- `stop()` routes the sentinel through `_send_stop`, which retries in 50ms slices while the thread is alive rather than issuing one blocking `put`. Without that, a bounded queue turns `stop()` into a deadlock in exactly the case case 3 covers: the thread has already exited on a producer-sent `STOP`, the queue is full, and nothing will ever free a slot.

The limit is on queued items, not concurrency: one thread means one callback at a time, so `max_pending=N` caps the backlog at N, with the in-flight item counted until `task_done()`. In case 1, six items through a 2-slot queue held the producer for 0.15s instead of returning immediately.

Two things this does not do. Backpressure is only as good as the producer — `put()` blocking means the producer's thread stalls, which is the point, but if that thread also serves something latency-sensitive you want `put(block=False)` and a drop policy instead. And `_send_stop` can still spin for the full `timeout` if the thread is alive and wedged inside a callback that never returns; the sentinel goes in as soon as a slot frees, but nothing preempts a hung callback. A hard cancel that drops the backlog remains unbuilt — still available if you want it.
